archetype.name: Bubble Team (goalie-and-PK propped)
archetype.definition: St. Louis is a coin-flip team at 5-on-5 that stays near the playoff line because of an elite penalty kill and one hot goalie, and it lacks the even-strength edge to climb out of the middle.

report.headline: Hofer and the penalty kill keep a break-even five-on-five team afloat
report.take:
The Blues at 7-8-2 are hard to fault and hard to like. Their underlying 5-on-5 play is dead average: a 49.6% xGF % (18th) and an exactly even 50% CF %. Their Goal Diff / GP of -0.18 sits 21st, which matches their 21st place on the Teams tab. The offense is the softer half, 21st in goals a game against 16th in goals allowed. Seventh in the Central with Chicago the only team below them is about what that profile earns.

What changed from last year is not the even-strength game. Last season's xGF % was .493, nearly the same. The movement came on special teams and in the crease. The power play went from 17.6% to 22.4%. The penalty kill went from 76.7% to 84.4%, 8th in the league and well above the 77% average. Goalies GSAx swung from -7.2 to a positive 1.2. That team total hides a sharp split: Joel Hofer has a .919 save % and +5.9 GSAx over 12 starts and sits 8th on the goalie tab. Jordan Binnington's five starts produced an .851 and -5.4, which nearly erased Hofer's work. The B+ goaltending grade belongs to Hofer.

The numbers hide two things working against each other. One is bad luck. Pts vs Goal Diff of -1.9 ranks 27th, so the record is a little worse than the goals imply. A 5-on-5 PDO of 98.3 and a 10.8% shooting rate, below the league's 11.6%, suggest some finishing will come back. The other is a real defensive problem. They give up 28.5 shots a game (25th) behind a C- blueline. Philip Broberg carries that group at nearly 25 minutes and ranks 17th on his tab. The next three by ice time, Cam Fowler, Colton Parayko and Brandon Carlo, all rank outside the top 150. Justin Barron is the best-rated of the rest (46th, .566 xGF %) on fewer minutes. Opposing centers are also feasting: Blues defenses rank 26th against them.

November has opened with three straight losses on two goals a game. With 65 games left, the pace of 77 points looks like the floor rather than the forecast. The goaltending split argues for more Hofer, the close-game luck should even out, and the forwards have three 12-point players. This is a team fighting for a wild-card spot, not one built to win a round. The shot volume against will cap it unless the defense pairs change.

strengths.title: A top-ten penalty kill
strengths.body: The kill is at 84.4%, well above the league average and a big jump from last year's 76.7%. It is the main reason a team giving up so many shots sits only mid-pack in goals against. Kills this far above average usually drift back somewhat, but the year-over-year change is too large to be pure noise.

strengths.title: Joel Hofer's goaltending
strengths.body: Hofer has a .919 save %, 5.9 goals saved above expected and a top-ten place on the goalie tab. He is the difference between this team and last year's -7.2 GSAx group. Only goalie performance this good can cover for the shot volume in front of him. Whether it lasts depends on how much of the net he gets.

strengths.title: Balanced forward scoring
strengths.body: Robert Thomas, Jimmy Snuggerud, Dylan Holloway and Mason McTavish all have 12 points. McTavish leads the forwards with 47 shots, and Snuggerud has 9 goals. The group is graded only a C, but scoring spread across lines means one cold player doesn't sink the offense. The power play's rise to 22.4% gives these players a second outlet.

concerns.title: Too many shots, thin defense
concerns.body: St. Louis allows 28.5 shots a game, 25th in the league and above the league's 27.0. The blueline is graded C-. Broberg is the only regular rated near the top of his tab, while the three defensemen playing the most minutes behind him rank outside the top 150. Unless Barron's minutes grow, this is a structural problem rather than a slump.

concerns.title: Centers are running free
concerns.body: Opposing centers produce 3.53 points a game against St. Louis, above the 3.06 their own averages predict, which ranks 26th. Centers take 41.1% of the points scored against the Blues, compared with 36.6% across the league. That points to the middle of the ice, not the wings or the back end, being the leak.

concerns.title: The goals have dried up
concerns.body: November has produced two goals a game, and the last ten games run well below the season's scoring rate. That stretch includes back-to-back shutout losses to Carolina and Montreal. Some of this is a 10.8% shooting rate that should rise toward the league average. But a break-even shot share doesn't guarantee the goals return.

trend.note: The season has swung between scoring bursts and blanks: two straight shutout losses, then two wins with nine goals, then three straight November losses. The last five games are actually a shade better than the season by points %, so this is choppiness rather than a collapse.

weekAhead.headline: Two leaky penalty kills, then Florida's possession game at home
weekAhead.body:
The week offers two chances for the improved power play. Detroit kills only 69% of its penalties and Utah 69.6%, both in the league's bottom five. Detroit, at home first, is a near-twin in the standings at 22nd on the site. The Red Wings out-chance opponents (8th in xGF %) but can't finish, shooting a league-worst 9.1% behind D+ goaltending. The Blues should take that game, though Detroit's 5-on-5 play is better than theirs.

Utah on the road is the hardest game. The Mammoth are 2nd in xGF %, carry A- forwards and an A blueline, and run the league's second-best power play at 37.1%. That power play meets the Blues' top-ten kill head-on. Utah's F-graded goaltending, at -12.8 GSAx, is the opening. Florida closes the week in St. Louis at 4th in CF %, a test for a blueline that already concedes too much volume. Two of the three opponents sit above the Blues on the site, so a split is the realistic target, with special teams deciding where it lands.

keyMatchups.title: Blues PK vs Utah's power play
keyMatchups.body: Utah converts 37.1% of its power plays, second in the league. St. Louis kills 84.4%, eighth. Whichever unit wins this likely decides the road game, because Utah's 5-on-5 share is far ahead of the Blues'.

keyMatchups.title: Shooters against weak goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Utah's goalies are 31st in GSAx, and Detroit's are graded D+ with a .886 save %. A Blues team shooting below the league average gets its best chance this week to fix that. Volume shooters like McTavish and Snuggerud should find openings.

keyMatchups.title: Florida's puck control at home
keyMatchups.body: Florida holds 55% of 5-on-5 shot attempts and limits opponents to 23.9 shots a game. The Panthers' 96.2 PDO says their results trail their play. Against a Blues defense already 25th in shots allowed, this could become a long night in their own end.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal: Hofer has carried the team, and any Binnington start is the week's biggest risk.

restOfSeason.body:
The 77-point pace understates this team. Pts vs Goal Diff should drift back toward zero, the 5-on-5 shooting should recover from a 98.3 PDO, and Hofer should keep the bulk of the starts. Those three things point to a finish somewhere between 80 and 88 points. That is roughly last season's 86, give or take, and right on the wild-card bubble in a deep Central.

What won't hold is the 84.4% penalty kill at that level; some drift down is likely. Hofer's .919 is also a hot start until he proves otherwise over a heavier load. The ceiling stays low as long as the team concedes this many shots and plays heavy minutes on low-rated defensemen. The best path to better results is pushing its 5-on-5 shot share above even, not hoping the goaltending stays this good.
swingFactors: Hofer's share of the starts and whether his save % holds
Whether the penalty kill stays in the top ten
Ice time for Barron over the lower-rated defensemen

confidence.note: Only 17 games in, and the goaltending and PK numbers rest on small samples. The 5-on-5 profile closely matches last season, which gives the read some stability.
